classification.difficultyReason: Select extreme subsets for the means, then recognise the unprompted integrality obstruction to a proposed mean rather than searching examples; the impossibility justification is the hardest essential demand.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the smallest and the largest sample mean obtainable from samples of 5.

answer.worked:
The five smallest values give the smallest mean; the five largest values give the largest mean.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Smallest mean}&=\frac{1+3+5+7+9}{5}\\\text{Smallest mean}&=5\\\text{Largest mean}&=\frac{9+11+13+15+17}{5}\\\text{Largest mean}&=13\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The average of the whole dataset is 9. Is there a sample of 5 which has a mean of 8.5?

answer.short: No. Its five values would need to sum to $42.5$, but all the supplied values are whole numbers.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Required sum}&=8.5\times5\\\text{Required sum}&=42.5\end{align*}$$

Any five values from the dataset have a whole-number sum, so their sum cannot be $42.5$. Such a sample is impossible.
